title: Project
text:
Several different methods are implemented to optimize the model (in a way of compression) and KV cache. First, we will explore LCLM (latent context language model) for inputs (during Encoder phase). Then, we apply random rotation on the key and use different bit quantizations on both keys and values with FP16 recent token window. Lastly, we apply MSE-optimized quantization and apply QJL residual correction on the error. (Random rotation, MSE-optimized quantization and QJL comes from the “TurboQuant”)
To mitigate the problem of extra variance from QJL, we will incorporate insights from matrix sketching (Especially, Hadamard transform).

title: DepthWeave-KV Paper Review
text: This page reviews the paper (Cordoba et al. 2026) published and submitted on July 2026.

title: DepthWeave-KV Paper Review
text:
What is DepthWeave-KV?
First of all, what does term “DepthWeave” represent?
If we separate the term Depth and Weave, it is easier to understand.
In a general transformer model, there is a sequence of transformer layers, also called a transformer block. Each layer has its own Query, Key and Value block, and each also has its own learned parameters.
The term “Depth” represents exactly this transformer layer. Since neighboring layers have a more impact on each other, the idea of combining the adjacent layers for a compression (Depth-wise) Compression is suggested.
Then, What is Weave? The term “Weave” in English is familiar when we think about threading for clothes, and this intuition also helps to understand the term “Weave” in the paper. It mainly represents how the method interaces shared information across transformer depth. The details of the method will be explained in the later section.
Therefore, “DepthWeave” broadly describes the weaving of representations across Transformer layers (“Weave”) along the model’s depth dimension (Depth).

title: DepthWeave-KV Paper Review
text:
Depth-wise Vs. DepthWeave
It is also crucial to acknowledge the difference between Depth-wise and DepthWeave KV compression.
The basic depth-wise compression only considers the similarity of KV states between adjacent transformer layers. For example, Suppose there are three neighboring layers \(X_{1,t}^Z, X_{2,t}^Z, X_{1,t}^Z\) where \(Z \in \{K, V\}\). Then, we can make them as one representative KV state or one shared low-ranked basis. Conceptually, combined representation can be \[\hat{X}_{l,t} = A_{l,t}B^Z\] where \(B^Z\) is the shared basis across three layers. (\(A_{l,t}\) here is the token and layer-specific coefficient)
On the other hand, Depthweave is a more flexible form of this depth-wise compression). In addition to the shared basis across layers, it also preserves the differences between layers and tokens. Conceptually, \[\hat{X}_{l,h,t}^Z = A_{l,h,t}^ZB^Z_{m,h} + g^Z_{l,h,t}R^Z_{l,h,t}\] where \(B^Z_{m,h}\) is the shared basis for a window of neighboring layers, \(A_{l,h,t}^Z\) is the coefficient specific to the layer and token, \(g_{l,h,t}^Z\) is a gate-controlling how much residual correction is applied and \(R_{l,h,t}^Z\) is the residual that restores information lost by shared basis. So, after aggregating adjacent layers in the same window \(m\), the token-specific residuals are given with a learned value of gate-controlling coefficient. (Here, \(h\) represents the attention head.)
So, DepthWeave not only considers the similarity between adjacent layers, but also controls the token-specific residual for a better accuracy.

title: DepthWeave-KV Paper Review
section: Limitations of Prior KV Compression Methods (mentioned in the paper)
text:
Limitations of Prior KV Compression Methods (mentioned in the paper)
There are two limitations of Prior KV compression Methods mentioned in the paper.
First, prior KV compression including token eviction, token merging, quantization, low rank attention and layer-wise cache sharing has reduced the KV-cache memory, but many of them rely on static or locally observed token-importance signal (ignore the fact that the unimportant current token can be important later). Also, since each layer encode different information, the same token is represented differently across transformer layers. And the paper mentions that “the transformer layers that encode shallow lexical anchors and deeper semantic abstractions do not require the same cache fidelity”. (But many of compression methods miss this fact)
Second, they specifically mentioned the “Depth-wise KV compression alone is insufficient for heterogeneous long-context workloads”. Since Depth-wise KV compression only considers the layer combination, it does not consider that “the same token can demand different treatment in early lexical layers and later semantic layers”.

title: DepthWeave-KV Paper Review
text:
Four Important Contributions

1. Cross-depth residual factorization
The shared basis channels per attention head (\(B^Z_{m,h}\)) are stored and layer-specific key/value states through lightweight learned residual gates (\(g^Z_{l,h,t}\)) are reconstructed.


2. Token-Conditional depth router
The depth router decides residual budget for a specific token. The allocation budget and rank is determined by this depth router. The paper describes practical residual rank-levels such as \(\rho \in \{0,2,4,8\}\). The \(\rho\) value is determined by the equation, \[\rho_{m,h,t} = \rho_{min}+(\rho_{max}-\rho_{min}) \cdot 1[\sigma (u^T\phi_{m,h,t})>\tau_m]\]
where \(\phi_{m,h,t}\) denotes the feature vector , \(u\) is a small learned router parameter shared across layers in the window, and \(\tau_m\) is an adaptive threshold chosen to satisfy the current memory budget.
Especially, the feature vector \(\phi_{m,h,t}\) represents the information about how important the token appear to be, and the paper uses online metadata features rather than running another full neural network model through the base model. Also, the router computes \(u^T \phi_{m,h,t}\), a weight combination of the features, and by applying sigmoid function, we can interpret \(\sigma(u^T\phi_{m,h,y})\) as token importance or high-rank routing score (if it is close to 1: safe to compress aggressively, if it is close to 0: needs a faithful residual). Finally, by using threshold value \(\tau_m\), we can determine the final value of residual rank-level \(\rho_{m,h,t}\).


3. Calibration-free online error tracking using attention-output probes
Normally, the rank-level \(\rho\) is determined with a calibration dataset (for example, given 1000 long context prompts, the rank-level for layer 24-27 is 8, …).
Instead, DepthWeave chooses a small subset of attention heads and a few recent query positions for every \(p\) decoing steps, and it observes the reconstruction error on the prompt currently being processed and adjusts its threshold \(\tau\) during generation.
By using the attention-output probes equation,
\[e_{l,h} = \frac{||Attn(Q_{l,h}, K_{l,h},V_{l,h})-Attn(Q_{l,h},\hat{K}_{l,h}, \hat{V}_{l,h})||}{||Attn(Q_{l,h}, K_{l,h}, V_{l,h})||_2+\epsilon} \]
The discrepency is measured, and depending on its value, the threshold \(\tau\) is adjusted.
(*Here, \(Attn(Q_{l,h}, K_{l,h}, V_{l,h})\) is computed from the higher fidelity reference which is created temporaily with a more accurate and less compressed method)


4. Fused CUDA Implementation
A fused CUDA implementation means that several operations that would normally runs on the separate GPU kernels are combined into one custom CUDA kernel.
For DepthWeave-KV, the fused kernel combines
\[ \scriptstyle
\text{Basis Lookup} \rightarrow \text{Coefficient Multiplication} \rightarrow \text{Residual Dequantization} \rightarrow \text{KV Reconstruction} \rightarrow \text{Attention Computation}\]
Instead of storing full Key and Value matrix in a global memory, it uses stored shared basis, basis coefficients, quantized residual components, residual quantization metadata, routing information and learned gate parameters to calculate the attention output.
Furthermore, since final attention output is a weighted sum of value vectors, the temporary value vector, \(\hat{V}_t\), can be discarded, and final attention output is calculated without storing and using full complete value matrix \(\hat{V}_{l,t}\).
The fused kernel ensures that these compressed bytes remain compressed until they are already inside the attention computation. The paper describes this as compression-aware execution.

title: DepthWeave-KV Paper Review
text:
Figure Explanation

The Figure 1 shows the overall operation of the Depthweave.
The figure assumes there are three depth regions (shallow lexical, middle bridge and deep semantic layers).
The blue curve represents shared basis for adjacent layers, and each different line shows the different low-rank basis channels.
The orange blocks indicates the residual budget for a token. Since the horizontal direction represents the token position, and the same token receives the same residual correction across depth, the orange blocks appear in the same horizontal positions across different regions.
The Depth router above roughly describes the residual budget decision method described before.
Online error probes presents the feedback mechanism that adjusts residual ranks during generation.

The figure 2 shows a more detailed mechanism of DepthWeave. It starts from three adjacent transformer layers and specifies each attention head from different layers.
Then, the shared basis for attention heads in the same position across the layers are determined.
The next step shows the learned gate coefficients (\(g\)) and the token-specific residual buffers from token-conditional depth router, and the Attention output calculation by using Fused CUDA operation described in the earlier section.

title: DepthWeave-KV Paper Review
section: Question regarding to the Residual Rank
text:
Question regarding to the Residual Rank
From the residual rank assignment, we can raise a question, ” which dimensions or channels are selected for residual correction?“(if \(\rho = 8\), then 8 dimensions or channels should be corrected.). Since the paper only describes how many channels are selected (\(\rho \in \{0,2,4,8\}\)), we have to decide which channels are corrected by residuals.
There are a few options we can assume for selecting raw head dimensions,

Largest residual magnitude
Choose \(S = \text{TopK}_j(|r_j|, \rho)\). This is the simplest method, and it exactly minimizes the coordinate-masking residual error \(||r-\tilde{r}||^2_2\) among all choices of \(\rho\) raw coordinates.
Variance-normalized magnitude
Some channels may naturally have much larger scales than others. Instead of using \(|r_j|\), use use \[s_j = \frac{|r_j|}{\sigma_{m,h,j}+ \epsilon}\]
where \(\sigma_{m,h,j}\) is the typical residual scale for that channel in the window and head.
Then, select \(S = \text{TopK}_j(s_j, \rho)\). This detects unusually large residuals relative to the channel’s normal behavior, rather than always selecting naturally high-variance dimensions.
Fixed channel ordering
Group or block selection

title: MOH: Multi-head Attention as Mixture of Heads
text: This page reviews the paper (Jin et al. 2025) published and submitted on Oct 2024.

title: MOH: Multi-head Attention as Mixture of Heads
text:
Improvement upon the Multi-Head Attention
The Multi-head Attention mechanism has multiple attention heads which operate in parallel, and the final attention outputs are calculated as the sum of all heads. To improve the efficiency (with maintaining the similar accuracy) of this mechanism, the paper proposes a selection mechanism for tokens to select appropriate attention heads (Dynamic Attention head Routing Mechanism).

title: MOH: Multi-head Attention as Mixture of Heads
text:
Mixture of Experts
The previous study, “Mixture of Experts (MOE)”, is the main motivation and methodology of this paper. It literally means that it chooses experts for a subset of model and combines those specialized subsets to process the information. Furthermore, it uses a special machine called a router which activates Top-K experts for each subset.

title: MOH: Multi-head Attention as Mixture of Heads
text:
Mixture of Heads
Motivated by the MOE, the paper introduces Mixture of Head Attention, “MOH”. Instead of parameters scaling in regular MOE, they chooses attention heads as experts. Similar to MOE, it consists of h heads, \(H = {H^1,...,H^h}\), and a router that activates the Top-K attention heads.

title: MOH: Multi-head Attention as Mixture of Heads
text:
More about Methodology

Heads as Experts
The MoH output can be calculated as
\[MoH(X, X') = \sum_{i=1}^h g_iH^iW^i_O\]
where \(X\) and \(X'\) are input tokens, \(g_i\) is the routing score, \(H_i\) is the output of \(i\)-th attention head, and \(W_O^i\) is that Head’s portion of the output projection.
Since \(g_i = 0\) when the head is inactive, the Top-K heads can be selected and activated based on the routing score.
There are two key advantages of MoH mentioned in the paper,

MoH enables each token to select the most relevant attention heads, boosting inference efficiency while maintaining accuracy
In contrast to the standard summation in multi-head attention, the weighted summation in MoH enhances the flexibility of the attention mechanism and unlocks performance potential.

It is easy to understand the first key advantage but a bit vague about the second statement.
why choosing a few heads instead of uniformly calculate all of them makes more flexibility, and what was the unresolved performance potential before MoH?
This can be answered by the details of methodology below.


Shared Heads
Among several attention heads, there are several heads that are always active for every token. The paper calls this as shared heads.
For \(h\) attention heads, we can define \(h_s\) as the number of shared heads, and \(h-h_s\) as number of routed heads.
\(H_1, ...,H^{h_s},H^{h_s+1},...,H^h\)
As it shows above, first \(h_s\) heads are chosen to be the shared heads, and the main purpose of the shared heads is to capture the global common knowledge such as basic grammar or punctuation markers.


Two-stage Routing
From the equation, \[MoH(X, X') = \sum_{i=1}^h g_iH^iW^i_O\]
There are actually two stages to determine the routing score.

Stage 1: Balance the two head types
The model computes \([\alpha_1, \alpha_2]=\text{Softmax}(W_hx_t)\)
where \(\alpha_1\) is the total importance assigned to shared heads group, and \(\alpha_2\) is the total importance assigned to routed heads group.
Stage 2: Weight or select heads inside each group
The shared heads receive the probabilities, \(p^{(s)} = \text{Softmax}(W_sx_t)\). Since shared heads are always active, their routing scores are calculated as \(g_{t,i} = \alpha_1 p^{(s)}\), \((1\leq i \leq h_s)\).
For the routed heads, the router computes \(p^{(r)} = \text{Softmax}(W_rx_t)\). Then only for Top-K routed heads, the routing scores are calculated as \(g_{t,i} = \alpha_2p^{(r)}\).
So, the routing score is the mixture of head-type importance and individual-head importance.
And this is also the main reason that MoH is flexible and increases its performance as it reflects the head-type importance and individual-head importance in a such way.



Load Balance Loss
Since MoH only selects Top-K routed heads, the router may repeatedly select the same few heads without additional control. For example, if it is Top-1 model, one of Heads (say, Head 1) receives most tokens, and rest of Heads may receive almost none.
We call this as routing collapse.
To mitigate such problem, the paper introduces load balance loss on routed heads only.
\[\mathcal{L}_b = \sum_{h_s+1}^h P_if_i\]
\[P_i = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T \text{Softmax}(W_rx_t)_{i-h_s}\]
\[f_i = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T 1(\text{Token $x_t$ selects Head $i$})\]
As it shows above, there are 3 equations for load balance loss.
\(T\) is the total number of tokens in the training batch.
\(P_i\) represents the average router probability assigned to Head \(i\) across the batch.
\(f_i\) measures the actual fraction of tokens selecting head \(i\) after Top-K routing.
If we rewrite the loss as \(\mathcal{L}_b = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_i f_i p_{t,i}\)
Then for one token router logit \(z_{t,j}\),
\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_b}{\partial z_{t,j}} = \frac{1}{T}p_{t,j}(f_j-\sum_if_ip_{t,i})\]

Overused Head
Suppose head \(j\) has a selection frequency larger than the probability-weighted average,
\[f_j > \sum_if_i p_{t,i}\]
Then
\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_b}{\partial z_{t,j}} > 0 \]
and gradient descent performs
\[z_{t,j} \leftarrow z_{t,j}-\eta\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_b}{\partial z_{t,j}}\]
so the head’s logit decreases. Its future routing probability also decreases.
On the other hand, head’s logit increases and future routing probability increases for underused heads.



Total Training Objective
\[\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L_{\text{task}}} + \beta \mathcal{L}_b \]
The toal objective is the summation of task loss \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{task}}\) and Balancing loss \(\mathcal{L}_b\) with a parameter \(\beta\).
The task loss may tell us “this head is particularly useful for this token”, and the balancing loss may tell us “this head is already receiving too many tokens across this batch”.
The parameter \(\beta\) controls the trade-off between them. Depending on the scale of \(\beta\), the routing can become highly specialized or balanced. In the paper, \(\beta\) is set to 0.01 for all tasks.

Some characteristics of Kimi K3

It also has native vision capabilities and 1 million token context length
It is built on Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) and Attention Residuals

title: Kimi K3 Paper Review
text:
Three complementary dimensions

Sequence Length: For sequence length, hybrid attention combines three Kimi Delta Attention layers with one Gated MLA layer in each block (efficient mechanism for long-context token mixing while retaining selective high-capacity attention).
Network Depth: Along the depth dimension, Attention Residuals (AttnRes) enable each module to selectively retrieve representations from embeddings, the current block, and proceeding blocks (extending information access beyond sequential residual accumulation)
Along the width dimension, each attention layer is followed by a stable LatentMoE layer that performs sparse channel mixing, effectively activating 16 of 896 routed experts for each token.

title: Kimi K3 Paper Review
section: More about Hybrid Attention (3 KDAs + 1 Gated MLA)
text:
More about Hybrid Attention (3 KDAs + 1 Gated MLA)

Kimi Delta Attention (KDA)
KDA extends the delta-rule recurrence with a channel-wise forget gate \[S_t = (I-\beta_tk_tk_t^T)\text{Diag}(\alpha_t)S_{t-1}+\beta_tk_tv_t^T\] \[ \tilde{o}_t = S_t^Tq_t \space \text{(output)}\] where \(\alpha_t \in (0,1)^{d_k}\) is the channel-wise one-step retention factor, and \(\beta_t \in (0,1)\) controls the delta-rule write strength
For channel-wise forgetting, it basically represents how much we retain each channel by using retention factor \(\alpha_t\).
\[\bar{S}_{t-1} = \text{Diag}(\alpha_t)S_{t-1}\]
where \[\text{Diag}(\alpha_t)=
\begin{bmatrix}
\alpha_{t,1} & 0 & \cdots \\
0 & \alpha_{t,2} & \cdots \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots
\end{bmatrix}\] Also, current prediction for \(k_t\) is \(\hat{V}_t = \bar{S}_{t-1}^Tk^t\).

More about Delta-rule
A basic Hebbian update for the memory \(S_t\) is \[S_t = \bar{S}_{t-1} + \beta_t k_t v_t\] It is very simple and straightforward, but the problem is that even if the approximate value \(\hat{v}_t\) is nearly correct, we need to compute the full vector \(v_t\) again, which can cause repeated information to be accumulated and interfere with other memories.
To mitigate this problem, we can use the prediction error \(e_t = v_t - \hat{v}_t\). Then, the memory update is \[S_t = \bar{S}_{t-1} + \beta_t k_t (v_t-\bar{S}_{t-1}^T k_t)^T \\ = \bar{S}_{t-1}+\beta_tk_tv_t^T - \beta_tk_tk_t^T\bar{S}_{t-1} \\ = (I- \beta_tk_tk_t^T) \bar{S}_{t-1} + \beta_t k_tv_t^T \\ = (I- \beta_tk_tk_t^T)\text{Diag}(\alpha_t) S_{t-1} + \beta_t k_t v_t^T\] which is exactly stated in the paper.
We can also notice that it is simply a one gradient step on:
\[L_t = \frac{1}{2}||\bar{S}_{t-1}^T k_t-v_t||^2 \\
\nabla_S L_t  = k_t(\hat{v}_t - v_t)^T\]
Therefore, \[ S_t = \bar{S}_{t-1} + \beta_t \nabla_S L_t = \bar{S}_{t-1} + k_t(\hat{v}_t - v_t)^T\]



So what does \(S_t\) represent?
\(S_t\) is simply a memory prediction. However, from the above illustration, we can view it in a more detailed way.
From delta rule, we acknowledge that it uses the error term (\(e_t\)) and also accounts for decayed old memory by using channel-wise forgetting factor \(\alpha_t\).
Thus, \(S_t = \text{decayed old memory} (\alpha_t) + \text{prediction error correction} (e_t)\)
In plain words, \(S_t\) stores the memory for old states (more memory to fresh states) and also prediction error for current prediction. So, we can use the flexible memory \(S_t\) to predict the current value for \(k_t\).


How KDA parameterizes
There are several parameters which KDA generates for the model (KDA parameterizes the per-head quantities),

\(q_t^h, k_t^h = L_2Norm(Swish(ShortConv(W_{q/k}^hx_t))) \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}\)
\(v_t^h = Swish(ShortConv(W_v^h x_t)) \in \mathbb{R}^{d_v}\)
\(\beta_t^h = Sigmoid(W_b^hx_t) \in (0,1)\)
\(z_t^h = W_{\alpha}^{\uparrow} W_{\alpha}^{\downarrow}x-t + b_\alpha^h \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}\)


Query and Key generation
\[q_t^h = k_t^h = L2Norm(Swish(ShortConv(W_{q/k}^hx_t))) \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}\]
The ShortConv (short convolution) involves current token and previous tokens by multiplying with their learned weights. For example, after query/key projection with the learned weights \(W_{q/k}^h\) and input \(x_t\),the ShortConv involves previous tokens to give more flexibility on feature extraction. (*new learnable weights: \(c_{i,t}\) for channel \(i\) and token i, and early query projection: \(q'_{t, i}\), Shortconv gives \(\tilde{q}_{t,i} = c_{i,0}q_{t,i}' + c_{i,1}q'_{t-1, i} + c_{i,2}q_{t-2, i}'\)).
Then, use Swish activation function which has advantages over Relu as it activates negative values.
Finally, we normalize (L2) these values for numerical stability.


Value generation
\[ Swish(ShortConv(W_v^hx_t)) \in \mathbb{R}^d_v\] Value generation is almost same as key/query generation except it does not normalize as we need magnitude of the values for the final feature extraction.


Delta-rule coefficient \(\beta_t^h\) generation

title: Biderctional vs. Causal masking (LCLM)
text:
From latent context language model (LCLM), the author highlights that (for encoder attention masking) LCLM performs better on Causal masking set-up than on bidirectional setting.
Since the bidirection makes query to look at entire context or every token, it is natural to think that bidirectional setting would be more accurate. However, the encoder is based on the pre-trained Qwen model which is trained under causal attention, and the pooling from causal attention gives useful hierarchical/accumulating structure to the latent vectors.
From these reasons, we can assume why causal attention performs better than bidirectional attention in LCLM.
To confirm these facts, we will investigate bidirectional and causal attention with pooling on small LCLM.

As it is illustrated in the setting and architecture, the only difference is the attention mask in encoder. The other settings are same for both models.

title: Biderctional vs. Causal masking (LCLM)
text:
About the Dataset…
To train and test the model, the needle retrieval task is chosen.
It is a very simple task to train and test the language model. First, we generate random tokens with a specific length (for example, it can be 5 random tokens: [32, 24, 52, 12, 97]). Then, we insert KEY in the random position (between numbers, for example: [32, 24, KEY, 52, 12, 97]). At the end, with a given query, we train the model to find the number comes after KEY.
In addition to the single needle retrieval task, the multi-key retrieval task is also implemented. It is basically same as the single needle retrieval task, but there are several keys in the sample, and the task is to find these keys with given queries (For example: [32,KEY_A, 24, KEY_B, 52, 12], QUERY_A and QUERY_B are the task to find the number comes after KEY_A and KEY_B accordingly.)
Also, before-key and before-after-key (Find number before KEY and find numbers which come before and after KEY) tasks are trained and tested for both models to verify whether the causal advantage is directly tied to the directionality.
So, the experiment looks like
\[\begin{array}{c}
\text{Single after-key Retrieval} \\[6pt]
\downarrow \\[6pt]
\text{Multi after-key Retrieval} \\[6pt]
\downarrow \\[6pt]
\text{Multi before-key Retrieval} \\[6pt]
\downarrow \\[6pt]
\text{Multi before-after-key Retrieval (accessorial task)}
\end{array}\] Since before-after task introduces extra changes at the same time: two targets instead of one, two output heads instead of one, a harder multitask objective, and a different loss, it becomes harder to know whether the cause was the encoder mask or simply the more difficult two-output task. So, we will focus more on the after-key and before-key Retrieval task.
(*For the multi before-after-key retrieval, it needs two heads structure for the model, the detailed model structure is illustrated in the Appendix.)

Result
For the Single after-key Retrieval task, both models (causal and bidirectional masks) show a high test accuracy and low test loss (1.0 and 0.001 accordingly).
For multi-key retrieval task, 6 different evaluations are measured during training and testing,

title: Different types of Quantization
text:
Uniform quantization
It is the basic type of quantization.
The quantized value of x can be calculated as
\[Q(x) = \Delta\cdot \text{round}(\frac{x}{\Delta})\]
where \(\Delta\) is the constant quantization step size.
It also emphasizes the defining property of unifrom quantization:
\[q_{i+1} - q_i = \Delta\]
The important part is that adjacent reconstruction levels are always separated by the same amount: \[ \Delta \]

title: Different types of Quantization
text:
Symmetric quantization
It is a special case of uniform quantization,
We rougly assume \[x_{min} \approx -x_{max}\]
Define \[ a= \text{max}|x|\] For signed b-bit quantization: \[Q_max = 2^{b-1}-1\]. Then, \[s = \frac{a}{Q_{max}}\] and \[q = \text{clip}(\text{round}(x/s), -Q_{max}, Q_{max}).\]
Reconstruction becomes: \[ \hat{x}=sq\]
It is very simple since \(x \approx sq\), and zero-point doesn’t need to be stored. However, since it forces to create the symmetric range, there would be many wasted levels if the original values are not distributed symmetrically.

title: Different types of Quantization
text:
Asymmetric/non-symmetric quantization
So, instead of forcing the range to be centred at zero, we use the actual range: \[[x_{min}, x_{max}]\]
For b bits:
\[ q_{min} = 0, q_{max} =2^b-1.\]
Scale:
\[s = \frac{x_{max}-x_{min}}{q_{max}-q_{min}}\]
Zero point:
\[z = \text{round}(q_{min} - \frac{x_{min}}{s})\]
Quantization:
\[q = \text{clip}(\text{round}(x/s)+z)\]
Reconstruction:
\[ \hat{x}=s(q-z).\]

title: Different types of Quantization
text:
Distinction between Uniform/non-uniform and Symmetric/asymmetric
Symmetric/asymmetric tells us where the quantization interval lies.
Uniform/non-uniform tells us how the levels are spaced.
So, we can have symmetric + uniform or asymmetric + uniform or even symmetric + non-uniform.
(Also, we can distinguish very easily by observing a zero-point \(z\) (for symmetric vs. asymmetric cases).)

text:
Several different methods are implemented to optimize the model (in a way of compression) and KV cache. First, we will explore LCLM (latent context language model) for inputs (during Encoder phase). Then, we apply random rotation on the key and use different bit quantizations on both keys and values with FP16 recent token window. Lastly, we apply MSE-optimized quantization and apply QJL residual correction on the error. (Random rotation, MSE-optimized quantization and QJL comes from the “TurboQuant”)
To mitigate the problem of extra variance from QJL, we will incorporate insights from matrix sketching (Especially, Hadamard transform).

title: Different types of Quantization
text:
Scalar and Vector quantization
All of the above quantization method can be scalar
For a vector \[ x=[x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4]\],
we quantize independently: \[Q(x) = [Q(x_1), Q(x_2), Q(x_3), Q(x_4)]\]
For vector quantization, instead of quantizing them independently, we treat \(\textbf{x}=[x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4]\) as one object.
If there’s a learned codebook \[C={c_1,c_2,..,c_M}.\] Each \(c_i\in \mathbb{R}^4\). Then choose \[i^*=\text{arg min}_i || \textbf{x}-c_i||_2^2\] Instead of storing four quantized integers, we store \(i^*\).
The advantage of vector quantization is that it captures correlation. For KV cache, dimensions are not necessarily statistically independent, so in principle: \[VQ(K)\] could outperform scalar INT4 at the same theoretical number of bits.
But the problem is that codebook lookup is significanlty harder and potentially slower.

title: Different types of Quantization
text:
Product quantization
Product quantization is similar to the vector quantiation. However, instead of calculating the whole dimensions, we split it into smaller dimensions. For example, for a key vector, \(K_t \in \mathbb{R}^64\), we split it: \[ K_t = [K_t^{(1)}, K_t^{(2)}, ... , K_t^{(8)}]\]. Then each subvector has dimension 8, and we independently ector quantize \[K_t^{(j)} \rightarrow c_{i_j}^{(j)} \]
and store \[[i_1, i_2,...,i_8]\]

title: Matrix Sketching
text:
Frobenius norm error

Definition 2 (Frobenius norm error) we will say a k-dimensional supspace of \(\mathbb{R}^d\) spans a \((1+\varepsilon)\) rank-k approximation to A if \[ ||A-ALL^T||_F \leq (1+\varepsilon)||A-A_k||_F\] where \(LL^T\) is the projection operator onto that subspace.

The textbook explains this by thinking each row of \(A\) as a data point, \(a_i\). If \(L \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}\) have orthonormal columns: \(L^TL = I_k\), then \(P_L=LL^T\) is the orthogonal projection matrix onto the subspace spanned by the columns of \(L\).
So, \(ALL^T\) means project every row of A onto the subspace \(L\), and therefore, \(A-ALL^T\) contains the projection error for every data point (row).
*The Frobenius norm \(||A-ALL^T||_F\) is the sum of all squared distances: \(||A-ALL^T||_F = \sum_{i=2}^n||a_i-P_La_i||_2^2\)
Also, \(A_k\) represents the best rank-k approximation to A obtained by truncated SVD. By Eckart-Young theorem, \(||A-A_k||_F = \text{min}_{\text{rank}(B) \leq k}||A-B||_F\).
So, \(||A-A_k||\) is the smallest possible rank-k error.
*The term \((1+\varepsilon)\) allows slightly worse solution.

Important Idea
Instead of knowing the ideal k-dimensional subspace, we find some larger subspace \(L \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\) perhaps of dimension \(r >k\).
Suppose, we’re guaranteed that somewhere inside \(L\) there exists a good k-dimensional subspace \(L_0 \subseteq L\) such that \(||A-P_{L_0}A||_F \leq (1+\varepsilon)||A-A_k||_F\).
Let \(P_L\) denote projection onto the larger space L. For one data point \(a_i\), it can be decomposed into \(a_i = P_La_i +a_i -P_La_i\).
Now, choose some candidate k-dimensional subspace \(L' \subseteq L\), we want to approximate \(a_i\) using \(L'\). The total error is \(a_i - P_{L'}a_i\)
\[a_i - P_{L'}a_i = (a_i-P_La_i) + (P_La_i - P_{L'}a_i)\] Notice that the first term \((a_i-P_La_i)\) is outside of the space \(L\), and the second term \((P_La_i - P_{L'}a_i))\) is inside the space \(L\).
Since these two vectors are perpendicular, we can use pythagorean theorem. \[||a_i-P_{L'}a_i||_2^2 = ||a_i-P_La_i||_2^2 + ||P_La_i - P_{L'}a_i||_2^2\] and by summing this over all rows \(a_i\): \[||A-P_{L'}A||_F^2 = ||A-P_LA||_F^2 + ||P_LA-P_{L'}A||_F^2\]
Since \(||A-P_LA||_F^2\) is fixed, minimizing \(||A-P_{L'}||_F^2\) is equivalent to minimizing \(||P_LA-P_{L'}A||_F^2\).


So… why is this matters for sketching?
Frequently, randomized algorithms first construct a relatively small space \(L\) such that \(L\) contains some good rank-k approximation. we may not know which k-dimensional directions are the correct ones yet. However, we can find the best rank-k approximation inside \(L\). So the workflow becomes \[A \rightarrow \text{Find a relatively small subspace L} \rightarrow \text{Project A as}\space AP_L \rightarrow \text{compute the best rank-k approximation inside L}\]
So, instead of solving the expensive low-rank problem directly in \(\mathbb{R}^d\), we first use sketching to discover a mush smaller candidate space.
